extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and advanced classical pianists and piano teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for classical piano technique, practice habits, memorization, interpretation, and teaching methods aimed at serious students and teachers seeking professional-level artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of touch and tone coloring
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes touches (melody touch expresses warmth and feeling; coloratura touch is sparkling, glittering, iridescent and made with arched hand and raised finger action) and emphasizes use of scale, arpeggio and coloratura touches to achieve tonal variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: melody touch = from the heart; coloratura = arched hand and raised finger action. Use down/up arm movements for chords; combine different touches to obtain tonal colors. Avoid one-dimensional 'big noise' playing that lacks tonal discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assimilation of touch principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle that 'when the player sees a certain passage, he knows at once what touch is required to express it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach and internalize the different touches so they become automatic like an actor's trained expression. The step beyond technical mastery is natural expressive performance; touches should be at the player's finger-tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorizing thoroughly and flexibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Require pieces to be so thoroughly memorized that if a measure or phrase is corrected the pupil can continue from that point without restarting from the beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept individual memorization methods (visual page, keyboard geography, ear-memory, harmonic memory); encourage learning away from the piano; recommend mental rehearsal of program before concerts. Practice committing music by phrases/ideas (one or two measures at a time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Octave study technique and endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the hand with the 'octave grimace' (arched hand, unemployed fingers slightly curved) and progress from short bursts to prolonged endurance work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with one beat in sixteenths and finish with a 'wiping off' touch; build longer groups of notes, play full length of keyboard in all keys and chromatically; can substitute four-voiced chords. Goal: prolong same exercise up to twenty minutes so octave passages become manageable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic repertoire upkeep
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize repertoire into sections/programs and review older pieces regularly to keep them 'in repair.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested weekly rotation by composer or category (e.g., Monday Chopin, Tuesday Schumann, then Liszt, Russian, modern composers, concertos, chamber music). Begin week with full run-through to identify weak spots and practice those.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily practice structure and priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocate practice time with a consistent plan: mornings for practice, afternoons for teaching; include at least one hour daily devoted to technical work (scales, arpeggios, octaves, chords, Bach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfect one selection of Bach by transposing into all keys and polishing thoroughly; prefer perfecting a few etudes deeply rather than superficially playing many. Quality of practice matters more than quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone-production training and listening
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone production is essential and neglected; pupils must be trained to listen and learn a variety of tonal qualities rather than merely producing notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement a special course in tone production alongside technical exercises from the start. Warn that the piano's ease in producing sound can foster carelessness; cultivate listening to every note and avoid 'bluff' loudness that impresses uncritical audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and metronome discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm (mechanical grouping and subtle rhythmic nuances) must be trained; use metronome practice to develop a reliable mechanical sense of rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize classes in ear-training and rhythm. For pupils with poor rhythm, daily metronome practice until improvement, then judiciously reduce use. Recognize that delicate rhythmic nuances (e.g., Chopin mazurka, Viennese waltz) may require inherent rhythmic gift in addition to training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leschetizky fundamentals: firm fingers and pliable wrist
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical foundation centered on two principles: firm fingers and pliable ('spring') wrist, established via hand formation and specific exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish arched hand, test finger/knuckle firmness by tapping (practice tapping at home). Begin wrist exercises early to avoid stiffness: raise/lower wrist supported on one to five fingers. The wrist should resist like a fine steel spring, capable of varying resistance according to tone demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legato vs. high finger action sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach legato touch before high finger action; for true legato play close to the keys without raising fingers high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High finger action is easier to teach later for non-legato and staccato work; beginning with high finger action can hinder developing a perfect legato. Reserve high finger action as a later stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of second piano and imitation in teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: A second piano in teaching is necessary so the teacher can demonstrate subtleties that cannot be conveyed by words alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher should constantly illustrate (e.g., swells, tonal and rhythmic nuance). Through imitation the pupil learns rapidly until their own individuality appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualized memorization methods
rubrics_metrics.description: No universal memorization rule; students should try various methods (visual of page, visual of keyboard, ear-memory, harmonic analysis) to discover what works best for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage familiarity with all strategies so the pupil can combine or select methods suited to their memory strengths. Mental rehearsal of entire program is recommended before concerts and travel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical conditioning for weak hands
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend gymnastic exercises morning and evening for pupils with weak hands and arms to build the physical strength needed for brilliant technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical strength is essential for virtuosity; regular simple exercises support long-term technical goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping technic 'in repair' through constant work
rubrics_metrics.description: Technic is mechanical and must be maintained constantly by regular, targeted exercises chosen for the player's mechanical needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify key exercises that maintain the player's mechanical well-being and incorporate them into daily routine. Plan weekly practice to balance technical upkeep with repertoire maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent public/private playing to incentivize growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular playing before others (publicly or privately) is the greatest incentive for keeping repertoire and advancing artistry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage frequent performance opportunities to motivate polishing repertoire and to build stage experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality over quantity in practice hours
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrated, absolutely focused practice (four to five hours max for advanced artists) is more effective than longer unfocused practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adele Aus der Ohe: four or at most five hours sufficient if used with absolute concentration. Emphasize understanding construction and meaning of passages before repetition to avoid vain repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting natural hand positions ('letting the hand find itself')
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rigidly enforce a single hand position; if a pupil produces good tone and effects, accept their present hand position and carry them forward rather than forcing discouraging change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liszt's idea: avoid changing an established natural position that would require long re-training. Recognize multiple legitimate hand positions; each hand is a separate study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique selection: simple exercises with principle focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical practice should use simple exercises where each contains a principle of touch, movement or condition rather than aimless complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include thumb-under/over work, different tonal qualities, staccato vs legato touches, scales, arpeggios and Bach as part of technic study; keep exercises connected to real musical problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power and velocity principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Gain power by practicing heavy chords and five-note combinations; acquire velocity by eliminating unnecessary movement and raising fingers minimally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For early stages and slow practice, raise fingers to ensure exactness. Leschetizky values finger action for finger development; balance finger action training with economy of motion for speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four artistic requisites for public pianists
rubrics_metrics.description: To make an artistic success in public, a pianist needs: variety of tone color; individual and artistic phrasing; true feeling; and personal magnetism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone color: use tonal 'colors' to paint pictures; phrasing: be artistic, not mechanical; true feeling: avoid dry, cut-and-dried performances; personal magnetism: stage presence matters to convey art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrasing surprises and climax treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of making the expected loud peak the focal point, consider making the highest point softer (making climaxes pianissimo) to create tonal surprises and deeper expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: build crescendo but soften the expected loudness at the apex to remove sharpness and produce unexpected tonal shading. Apply especially to lyric playing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn tone/color from singers and opera
rubrics_metrics.description: Pianists should study great singers and opera to learn tone production, color, effect, light and shade, and emotional action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearing a great singer provides exemplars of breath-driven phrasing and vocal color that inform piano tone production. Attend concerts and opera as a means of education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical uniformity; play with true feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: A true artist must never give mechanical performances that are identical every time; variability and authenticity of feeling are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A performer cannot 'feel the same twice,' so performances will and should differ; stay within artistic bounds but allow expressive freedom. Mechanical uniformity kills inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breath control during performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain easy, natural respiration; for fortissimo and difficult passages, keep lips closed and breathe through the nostrils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breath control supports physical exertion without disrupting musical line; integrate respiration into phrasing and stamina planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher selectivity and attention to detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer intelligent, advanced pupils; be particular about hand position and touch, and work in detail with advanced students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissect details in lessons and refine hand position and touch where necessary; choose pupils likely to benefit from intensive, detailed guidance.
